title: Physical Models of Living Systems
text:
0.1 Scope
These are lecture notes for Physical Models of Living Systems (third-semester elective, Master in Physics of Data, University of Padova, instructor Prof. Samir Suweis). The course uses the vocabulary of statistical physics — master equations, mean-field limits, phase transitions, random matrices, criticality — to model biological systems at scales that span from a single microbial population to a whole brain.
The notes are split into two halves that mirror the course:

title: Physical Models of Living Systems
text:
Ecology. How to write down and analyse a model of one, few, or many species living, reproducing and interacting. Deterministic and stochastic descriptions of population growth; neutral theory and macroecological patterns; the Lotka–Volterra family; random-matrix results on the complexity–stability trade-off.
Neural systems. Firing-rate models for populations of neurons; Hebbian plasticity and associative memory (Hopfield networks); the Boltzmann machine as a probabilistic recurrent network; and the hypothesis that healthy brain dynamics live near a critical point.

title: Physical Models of Living Systems
text:
0.2 Reading the notes
Every chapter is self-contained enough that it can be read on its own, but the two halves share a common toolbox: master equations and the Fokker–Planck / Langevin limit appear in ecology (Chapter 2) and again in neural dynamics (Chapter 5–7); the notion of a phase transition and of scaling laws frames both the neutral theory of biodiversity (Chapter 3) and brain criticality (Chapter 7).
Definitions, theorems, worked examples and remarks are collected in styled callouts so the key results can be scanned without reading through the derivations.

title: Physical Models of Living Systems
text:
0.3 Notation

\(n(t), N(t)\): population size (single species / community total).
\(\rho(\mathbf x, t)\): probability density on state space; \(P_n(t)\) its discrete counterpart.
\(\mathcal{L}\): master-equation generator; \(D(x)\) and \(A(x)\) drift and diffusion in Fokker–Planck.
\(r_i, K_i, \alpha_{ij}\): intrinsic growth rate, carrying capacity, and pairwise interaction coefficient in Lotka–Volterra.
\(\phi_i(t)\): firing rate of neuron / population \(i\); \(W_{ij}\) synaptic weight.
\(\mathbf s = (s_1, \ldots, s_N)\): Boolean neural state (\(s_i \in \{0,1\}\) or \(\{\pm 1\}\)).
\(H[\mathbf s]\): energy function of a Hopfield / Boltzmann network; \(\beta = 1/T\) inverse temperature.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Two motivating examples
This chapter follows the opening of Prof. Suweis’s notes. It uses two motivating examples — the collapse of the Atlantic cod fishery and the geographic distribution of malaria mortality — to introduce the vocabulary the rest of the course will rely on: emergent property, critical transition, power law, and universality.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
The record of cod catches in the Atlantic Ocean over the twentieth century shows regular oscillations that track reproduction cycles, plus one enormous peak in the mid-1960s driven by industrial fishing. That peak is followed by a smaller local maximum and then a sharp collapse in the early 1990s — the population never recovered. The abruptness of the collapse (rather than the smooth decrease a naive linear model would predict) is what makes this a critical transition. Explaining such abrupt changes is one of the main threads of the course.


A worldwide map of deaths caused by malaria shows a strongly non-uniform, patchy geography. Two possible statistical models describe such spatial data. A Gaussian model captures approximately uniform distributions with concentrated variance. A power-law model captures strongly heterogeneous distributions with fat tails. Understanding which parameters push a population toward one shape or the other is a recurring question in ecology.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.2 Emergent ecological patterns

An emergent property of an ecosystem is a universal feature of the system as a whole — not deducible from any single species or component — that arises as a collective behaviour of the entire structure. When the same pattern is observed for many taxa across many continents it typically signals a universal law underlying the property.

Three empirical patterns dominate the field:

The species–area relationship is the empirical scaling \(S(A) \propto A^{z}\), where \(S(A)\) is the number of species observed in an area \(A\) and \(z\) is a dimensionless exponent. The relationship holds across taxa (amphibians, birds, mammals) and across continents; only the multiplicative prefactor changes, not \(z\).


The endemic–area relationship is the analogous scaling \(E(A) \propto A^{z'}\) for the number of endemic species — those found only in the sampled area \(A\). Its exponent \(z'\) is close to \(1 - z\) in most datasets.


The relative species abundance is the empirical distribution of species abundances in a community. Preston’s log-normal and Fisher’s log-series are the two standard fits; either shape is remarkably robust across ecosystems.


Remark. The universality of SAR, EAR and RSA across ecosystems is one of the empirical strongholds of theoretical ecology. It is the reason why neutral theory (Chapter 3) — which reproduces all three patterns from a single mechanism — was received as a paradigm shift when it was proposed in the early 2000s.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.3 Scope of the course
The scientific goal is threefold: (i) understand why regular patterns emerge in systems with heterogeneous components and noisy dynamics; (ii) identify the fundamental mechanisms responsible; (iii) predict how the patterns respond to perturbations (climate, extinction, disease).
The methodological answer is the toolbox of statistical physics — master equations, mean-field limits, phase transitions, random matrices, criticality — applied to biological systems. Chapters 2–4 build the ecology half of the toolbox, and Chapters 5–10 build the neural systems half.

A physics-of-biology model is likely to be predictive when the system satisfies three conditions:

many degrees of freedom (\(N \gg 1\)),
local, sparse, or mean-field interactions,
some form of noise (thermal, demographic, synaptic) that makes ensemble averages well defined.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.4 Critical transitions
The cod fishery collapse is one instance of a general phenomenon: some systems undergo qualitative changes in their macroscopic behaviour as a control parameter is varied, and the change can be discontinuous.

A critical transition is a qualitative change in the macroscopic behaviour of a system that occurs at a critical value of some control parameter. At the transition point observables (order parameters, correlation lengths, response functions) show universal scaling, and small perturbations can have disproportionately large effects.


Remark (Physical meaning). Critical transitions in ecology (fishery collapse, forest–savanna shift, coral bleaching) mirror those in physics (magnetisation, superfluid transition). This parallel is not merely rhetorical: near a critical point the systems really are in the same universality class, share the same critical exponents, and can be analysed with the same renormalisation-group tools.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.5 Book supplements
The single most useful supplementary reference is Volkov, Banavar, Hubbell & Maritan, Neutral theory and relative species abundance in ecology, Nature 424, 1035 (2003), which lays out all three empirical patterns and shows how one mechanism explains them. On critical transitions in ecology, Marten Scheffer’s Critical Transitions in Nature and Society (Princeton, 2009) is a comprehensive treatment.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.6 Exercises

Verify that a SAR of the form \(S(A) \propto A^z\) implies a species–individual relationship \(S(N) \propto N^{z}\) if abundance is proportional to area. State the assumptions.


Solution. If \(N \propto A\) (density is spatially constant), then substituting \(A \propto N\) into \(S \propto A^z\) gives \(S \propto N^z\) with the same exponent. The result relies on the assumption of spatial homogeneity of the abundance density; when that fails (as in strongly clumped populations) the two exponents diverge.


For the Fisher log-series RSA, the number of species with \(k\) individuals is \(\phi_k = \theta x^k / k\) with parameters \(\theta, x < 1\). Show that the total number of species is \(S = -\theta \ln(1 - x)\) and the total number of individuals is \(J = \theta x/(1 - x)\).


Solution. \(S = \sum_{k \ge 1} \theta x^k/k = -\theta \ln(1 - x)\) (Taylor series of \(\ln\)). \(J = \sum_{k \ge 1} k \phi_k = \theta \sum_{k \ge 1} x^k = \theta x/(1 - x)\) (geometric series). Eliminating \(x\) recovers the fundamental biodiversity number \(\theta = J / \ln(J/S)\) for large \(J/S\).

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.7 Callouts






The introduction is largely phenomenological. Definitions of SAR, EAR, RSA are made precise here so the mathematical developments in Chapters 3–4 can be tested against them.









Whenever you see a scaling law in the field, check its exponent first: universal exponents point to universal mechanisms; system-specific exponents point to system-specific biology. This is the physicist’s first triage step.









The cod-fishery example is a paradigm of a regime shift, not a smooth decline. Statistical tests for regime shifts (Cusum, Bayesian change-point) differ from tests for gradual trends. Applying trend tests to shift data misses the phenomenon.

title: 3  Dynamics of a single species
text:
3.1 2.1 Population dynamics: exponential and logistic growth
This chapter follows Prof. Suweis’s Chapter 2. It builds from the simplest ecological model — a single bacterial population — up to a stochastic description that captures demographic noise. The four subsections mirror the source: (i) exponential and logistic growth from cell-division kinetics; (ii) the consumer–resource model and the quasi-stationary approximation; (iii) the stochastic birth–death master equation and its Fokker–Planck / Langevin limits; (iv) the stationary distribution and stochastic doubling time.
The paradigmatic microbial system is E. coli in a chemostat. Under the microscope a single bacterium grows up to a critical size and then divides into two — a cascade reproduction process. In optimal conditions the reproduction time is \(\tau \approx 20\) minutes.
The resource-limited fix is Verhulst’s:
crumbs: 3  Dynamics of a single species

title: 3  Dynamics of a single species
text:
Let \(N(t)\) be the population size at time \(t\). If per-capita reproduction happens at rate \(\mu\), the deterministic mean-field law is \[\frac{dN}{dt} = \mu N \implies N(t) = N(0)\,e^{\mu t} = N(0)\,2^{t/T},\] with doubling time \(T = \ln 2 / \mu\). For E. coli in optimal conditions \(\mu \approx 2.1\,\mathrm{h}^{-1}\), so \(T \approx 20\) min.


Remark. Two implicit assumptions: (i) \(N\) is treated as a continuous variable, which is a poor approximation for \(N \sim O(1)\) near \(t = 0\); (ii) resources are assumed unlimited. Removing (ii) is what motivates the logistic model below.



With carrying capacity \(k > 0\) the density-dependent update is \[\frac{dN}{dt} = \mu N\left(1 - \frac{N}{k}\right),\] whose explicit solution is \[N(t) = \frac{N(0)\,e^{\mu t}}{1 + \tfrac{N(0)}{k}(e^{\mu t} - 1)} .\] The two fixed points are \(N^* = 0\) (unstable if \(\mu > 0\)) and \(N^* = k\) (stable).


A batch culture of E. coli fits the logistic law until nutrients deplete. The lag phase corresponds to \(N \ll k\) where \(N(t) \approx N(0)\,e^{\mu t}\); the plateau corresponds to \(N \to k\). Fitting \(\mu\) and \(k\) from an OD-600 curve is one of the first assays a biophysics student runs.


3.1.1 2.1.1 Consumer Resource Model
Rather than encoding resource limitation in an ad-hoc carrying capacity, we can model the resource \(R(t)\) explicitly. Let \(g(R)\) be the resource uptake rate per unit cell and \(\mu(R)\) the growth-resource function. With uptake efficiency \(c\), yield coefficient \(\gamma\) (number of nutrient units to produce a bacterium), and death rate \(d\):

\[\frac{dN}{dt} = (\gamma c\,g(R) - d)\,N, \qquad \frac{dR}{dt} = \mu(R) - c\,g(R)\,N .\]

To get a closed-form population equation, assume the resource equilibrates much faster than the consumers (the quasi-stationary approximation, QSA): set \(dR/dt = 0\) and eliminate \(R\). For a biotic resource with logistic dynamics of its own, \(\mu(R) = R r^*(1 - R/k_c)\), algebra gives an effective logistic law
\[\frac{dN}{dt} = N\,(\tilde k - \tilde a N),\]
with effective growth rate \(\tilde k\) and effective saturation \(\tilde a\) built from the microscopic constants \(\{s, \mu, c, e, m\}\).

In the quasi-stationary limit of the consumer–resource model the population dynamics reduce to \[\dot N = r\,N(1 - N/K) + O(N^2),\] with \(r\) and \(K\) explicit combinations of the microscopic rates. The logistic law of §2.1 is thus a derived description, not a phenomenological guess.
crumbs: 3  Dynamics of a single species

title: 3  Dynamics of a single species
text:
3.2 2.2 Stochastic modelling of population growth
The deterministic ODE ignores the discreteness of individuals and the demographic noise that comes with it. Both matter when \(N\) is small.

3.2.1 2.2.1 Birth–death master equation

Let \(P_n(t)\) be the probability the population is \(n\) at time \(t\), with per-cell birth rate \(b_n\) and death rate \(d_n\). The master equation is \[\frac{dP_n(t)}{dt} = b_{n-1} P_{n-1}(t) + d_{n+1} P_{n+1}(t) - (b_n + d_n) P_n(t) .\] The right-hand side is gain minus loss of probability at state \(n\).

For the linear case \(b_n = bn\), \(d_n = dn\), the moments obey closed equations.

Starting from \(n(0) = n_0\), \[\langle n(t)\rangle = n_0\,e^{(b-d)t}, \qquad \text{Var}[n(t)] = n_0\,\frac{b+d}{b-d}\bigl(e^{2(b-d)t} - e^{(b-d)t}\bigr).\] The Fano factor \(F = \text{Var}[n]/\langle n\rangle\) grows without bound whenever \(b > d\): fluctuations are strongly super-Poissonian.



3.2.2 2.2.2 Fokker–Planck and Langevin equations
Rescaling \(n = \Omega x\) with \(\Omega \gg 1\) and expanding the master equation to second order gives the system-size expansion (Kramers–Moyal):

In the limit of large system size \(\Omega\), \[\partial_t \rho(x, t) = -\partial_x[A(x)\rho] + \frac{1}{2\Omega}\partial_x^2[B(x)\rho],\] with drift \(A(x) = \lim_{\Omega \to \infty}\Omega^{-1}(b_{\Omega x} - d_{\Omega x})\) and diffusion \(B(x) = \lim \Omega^{-1}(b_{\Omega x} + d_{\Omega x})\). The corresponding (Itô) SDE — the Langevin equation — is \[dx = A(x)\,dt + \sqrt{B(x)/\Omega}\,dW_t .\]

For the logistic birth–death process (\(b_n = bn\), \(d_n = dn + qn^2/K\)) one finds \(A(x) = rx(1-x)\) and \(B(x) = (b+d)x\).


3.2.3 2.2.3 Random walk
Close to the extinction boundary \(x \approx 0\), the drift is \(A \approx rx\) and the diffusion \(B \approx (b+d)x\), so \[dx \approx r x\,dt + \sqrt{(b+d)x/\Omega}\,dW_t .\] A Lamperti-type transform \(y = 2\sqrt{x\Omega/(b+d)}\) maps this to a biased random walk: \[dy = \tilde r\,dt + dW_t.\]

Setting \(r = 0\) (\(b = d\)) makes the walker unbiased. Standard random-walk theory shows that a walker on the half-line with a reflecting or absorbing barrier at 0 hits 0 with probability one: the population is extinct almost surely, even though its mean is conserved.



3.2.4 2.2.4 Stationary solution with linear rates
For a birth–death process satisfying detailed balance the stationary distribution is a product of rate ratios: \[P^{ss}_n = P^{ss}_0 \prod_{k=1}^{n} \frac{b_{k-1}}{d_k} .\]

For \(b_n = bn\) and \(d_n = dn + qn^2/K\) the stationary distribution has mode near the deterministic fixed point \(n^* = K(1 - d/b)\), with variance \(O(K)\). In the deterministic limit \(K \to \infty\) the distribution concentrates at \(n^*\).



3.2.5 2.2.5 Stochastic doubling
For a linear birth–death process with \(b > d\) the mean doubling time is \[\tau_2 = \ln 2 / (b - d),\] independent of \(n_0\). The fluctuations have coefficient of variation \[\frac{\sigma_{\tau_2}}{\tau_2} \sim \sqrt{\frac{b + d}{n_0\,(b - d)}} ,\] so relative fluctuations matter only for small populations. This is why single-cell lineage-tracking experiments see a broad distribution of division times.

Remark (Physical meaning). The three levels of description — master equation, Fokker–Planck, Langevin — are the same process at different resolutions: the master equation is exact but discrete; the Fokker–Planck retains fluctuations of order \(\Omega^{-1/2}\); the deterministic ODE \(\dot x = A(x)\) keeps only the drift. Going up the ladder trades tractability for exactness.

title: 3  Dynamics of a single species
text:
3.3 Exercises

Solve the logistic ODE explicitly. Verify that \(N(t) \to K\) as \(t \to \infty\) for any \(N_0 > 0\).


Solution. Separate variables: \[\frac{dN}{N(1 - N/K)} = \mu\,dt .\] Partial-fraction expand the left-hand side, integrate, and exponentiate to obtain \[N(t) = \frac{K}{1 + (K/N_0 - 1)e^{-\mu t}} .\] For \(\mu > 0\) the exponential decays, so \(N(t) \to K\).


Show that the linear birth–death process with \(b = d\) has \(\langle n(t)\rangle = n_0\) but \(\text{Var}[n(t)] = 2 b n_0 t\). Interpret the ratio \(\sigma / \langle n\rangle\).


Solution. Set \(b = d\) in the mean/variance formulas and take the limit \(b - d \to 0\) using l’Hôpital. Variance grows linearly in time: the Fano factor grows as \(2bt\), so relative fluctuations grow without bound. A critical branching process eventually goes extinct with probability one even though its mean is conserved.


Derive the QSA effective logistic law from the biotic consumer–resource system. Identify \(r\) and \(K\) explicitly in terms of \(\{r^*, k_c, c, \gamma, d\}\).


Solution. Setting \(\dot R = 0\): \(R^* = k_c(1 - cN/r^*)\). Substituting into \(\dot N/N = \gamma c R^* - d\) gives \(\dot N = N(\tilde k - \tilde a N)\) with \(\tilde k = \gamma c k_c - d\) and \(\tilde a = \gamma c^2 k_c / r^*\). Matching with the standard \(\dot N = rN(1 - N/K)\) yields \(r = \tilde k\) and \(K = \tilde k / \tilde a = r^*(\gamma c k_c - d)/(\gamma c^2 k_c) = r^*(1 - d/(\gamma c k_c))/c\).

title: 3  Dynamics of a single species
text:
3.4 Callouts






The logistic law is a phenomenological summary of many microscopic mechanisms (nutrient limitation, quorum sensing, waste build-up). Fitting a curve to it does not identify a mechanism.









Whenever a deterministic ODE has a fixed point at \(n^* = 0\) and a birth term proportional to \(n\), extinction has finite probability at all finite \(n_0\). Deterministic stability is not the same as stochastic survival.









When simulating a stochastic birth–death process, use the Gillespie algorithm rather than a discretised Langevin scheme for small \(n\): the Gillespie algorithm samples the exact interarrival distribution and preserves integer \(n\).









The Fokker–Planck limit assumes \(\Omega \gg 1\): it fails near extinction (\(n \ll \Omega\)). If you care about extinction probabilities, go back to the master equation.









Fitting parameters \((r, K)\) from data by nonlinear least squares often looks fine but hides large uncertainties: the correlation between \(r\) and \(K\) in the logistic fit is close to \(\pm 1\) unless the early exponential phase is well-sampled.

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.1 Motivation: from bacteria to forests
Real ecosystems host many species at once, and a lot of ecology consists in trying to explain the macroecological patterns — species-abundance distributions, species–area relationships, β-diversity across sites — that are seen empirically in almost every biome. This chapter introduces the classical neutral theory of Hubbell, in which those patterns are generated without any biological interaction: only birth, death and immigration acting on ecologically equivalent species.
A striking empirical fact is that the shape of the species-abundance distribution (SAD) — the histogram of the number of species with \(k\) individuals in a community — is remarkably similar across systems as different as tropical forests, coral reefs, and microbial communities. This suggests either (i) a fine-tuning of biological parameters across all ecosystems (unlikely), or (ii) an emergent statistical mechanism that is largely insensitive to the details.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
An ecological community satisfies the neutral hypothesis when all species share identical per-capita birth, death, and dispersal rates. Individuals are drawn from a common label pool but are otherwise interchangeable.


Remark (Physical meaning). The neutral hypothesis is a null model in the same sense that an ideal gas is a null model for a fluid. Every deviation from neutral predictions is a signature of biology (differential fitness, niche structure, competition).
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.2 The Hubbell model
Fix a community of exactly \(J\) individuals. At every time step: one individual dies at random, and it is replaced by (a) a copy of another individual drawn uniformly with probability \(1 - m\), or (b) a fresh migrant drawn from an external metacommunity with probability \(m\). This is a zero-sum Moran-like process with immigration.

In the neutral zero-sum model with metacommunity biodiversity number \(\theta\) and immigration rate \(m\), the expected number of species with \(k\) individuals in the local community of size \(J\) is given by \[\langle S_k \rangle = \theta \, \frac{J!\,\Gamma\bigl(k + I\bigr)\,\Gamma\bigl(J - k + I(1 - m^{-1})\bigr)}{k!\,(J - k)!\,\Gamma\bigl(I\bigr)\,\Gamma\bigl(J + I\bigr)}\cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\theta + I - \theta\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\theta\bigr)} ,\] where \(I = m(J-1)/(1-m)\). The functional form is a zero-sum multinomial whose limiting shape for \(m \to 0\) is Fisher’s log-series, and for \(m \to 1\) is a truncated log-series with heavier abundant-tail.

The result is somewhat unwieldy but its message is clean: two adjustable parameters \((\theta, m)\) are enough to reproduce SADs across many empirical datasets. That is a strong argument for neutral dynamics as an organising principle, though not for its literal truth.

The 50-hectare forest plot on Barro Colorado Island (Panama) contains \(\sim 21{,}000\) trees of \(\sim 300\) species. Fitting the Hubbell SAD to the observed abundance histogram gives \(\theta \approx 50\), \(m \approx 0.09\); the fit is essentially indistinguishable from a much more detailed niche-based model. This is the empirical result that made neutral theory famous.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.3 Scaling and criticality
The neutral community sits at a critical point in the parameter space: fluctuations in species abundances are power-law-tailed, and the correlation length (the typical range over which two individuals are related) diverges as \(m \to 0\). The physicist’s diagnostic is that observables scale as power laws in system size.

A quantity \(Q\) scales with system size \(L\) if \(Q(L) \sim L^\gamma\) for some exponent \(\gamma\) in the asymptotic regime \(L \to \infty\). Different observables sharing a small number of exponents that satisfy consistency relations define a universality class.


Under neutral dynamics on a lattice with dispersal length \(\ell\), the number of species found in an area \(A\) scales as \[S(A) \sim A^z, \qquad z \approx 0.25 \pm 0.1,\] independent of the microscopic diffusion. The exponent \(z\) is a critical exponent — it depends on spatial dimensionality and the tail of the dispersal kernel, not on the specific species.


The number of species endemic to (i.e. found only in) an area \(A\) scales as \(E(A) \sim A^{z'}\) with \(z' \sim 1 - z\). This is the theoretical prediction that lets conservation biologists estimate how many species would be lost if a patch of habitat of area \(A\) were destroyed.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.4 Phenomenological renormalisation group
A powerful test that a system is at a critical point is that its macroscopic distribution is scale invariant: coarse-graining leaves the shape of the SAD unchanged, only rescaled. The phenomenological RG procedure of Suweis et al. (2020) is to (i) partition a large empirical community into \(b\) sub-communities of equal size, (ii) compute the SAD of a randomly chosen sub-community, (iii) rescale abundances by \(\langle n \rangle\) and species counts by \(\langle S\rangle\). If the resulting distributions collapse across values of \(b\), the community is scale-invariant — as is observed for tropical forests and reef fish.

If the SAD \(P(n)\) collapses under the coarse-graining \(n \to n/b\), \(P \to b P\), then it is a power law: \(P(n) \sim n^{-\alpha}\) with \(\alpha\) determined by the way \(\langle n\rangle\) scales with \(b\).
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.5 Inferring biodiversity from presence–absence data
In many ecological surveys the raw datum is not abundance but presence–absence: for each of \(N\) sites and each of \(S\) species, one bit says whether the species was seen at the site. Recovering the full SAD from presence–absence is a classical inference problem.

Under the neutral assumption, the probability that species \(\sigma\) is present at a site of size \(J\) given it has abundance \(n_\sigma\) in the metacommunity is \[p_\sigma^{pres} = 1 - \bigl(1 - n_\sigma / J_M\bigr)^J .\] Inverting the relation with a beta prior on \(n_\sigma / J_M\) recovers the underlying \(\theta\) from presence–absence alone. This is how tropical biodiversity is estimated from herbarium records.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.6 Local dynamics and migration
Neutral theory can be extended to a spatial community, where individuals disperse over a distance drawn from a kernel \(K(\mathbf x)\). The kinetic equation for the density \(\rho_\sigma(\mathbf x, t)\) of species \(\sigma\) is a spatial birth–death–diffusion process. In the mean-field limit, \[\partial_t \rho_\sigma = D \nabla^2 \rho_\sigma + (b - d)\rho_\sigma - c\,\rho_\sigma\,\sum_{\sigma'} \rho_{\sigma'} + m\,\bar\rho_\sigma ,\] with the last term representing migration from the metacommunity mean \(\bar\rho_\sigma\).

For a single species with \(b > d\), transformed variables allow the extinction time \(T_{ext}\) to be computed as a first-passage problem for a biased random walk. In the large-\(K\) limit, \[\langle T_{ext}\rangle \sim K \exp\bigl(2K(b-d)/(b+d)\bigr),\] i.e. exponential in the carrying capacity — extinction is rare but not impossible.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.7 Grand canonical formulation
Just as in statistical mechanics one goes from the microcanonical to the canonical to the grand-canonical ensemble by relaxing conservation laws, neutral theory can be reformulated with a fluctuating total community size \(J\). The grand-canonical partition function admits a saddle-point evaluation and reproduces all the closed-form results above from a single generating functional.

Remark. The grand-canonical route is not mere formalism: it is what lets you compare SADs across datasets of different total abundance, and to define intensive quantities (diversity per unit area, species-per-individual ratio) that are the actual observables reported in the field.
crumbs: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.8 Exercises

The metacommunity in the Hubbell model has \(S_M\) species and total abundance \(J_M\). Show that the fundamental biodiversity number \(\theta = J_M / \ln(J_M/S_M)\) in the limit \(J_M \to \infty\) with \(S_M \to \infty\) fixed by the ratio.


Solution. Assume the metacommunity SAD is a Fisher log-series with parameter \(\theta\): \(\langle S_k\rangle = \theta x^k / k\) where \(x\) is chosen so that \(\sum_k k \langle S_k\rangle = J_M\). Sum the geometric series to obtain \(J_M = \theta x / (1 - x)\) and total species count \(S_M = -\theta \ln(1 - x)\). Eliminating \(x\) under \(x \to 1\) gives \(\theta = J_M / \ln(J_M / S_M)\) to leading order.


Verify that the species–area exponent \(z = 0.25\) predicted by neutral theory in \(d = 2\) is consistent with a random dispersal kernel of Gaussian form. What changes if the kernel is instead long-tailed (fat-tail exponent \(\mu\))?


Solution. With a Gaussian dispersal kernel of variance \(\ell^2\), the effective community size in an area \(A\) is \(A/\ell^2\), and the neutral scaling of the SAD gives \(S \sim (A/\ell^2)^{1/4}\). For a power-law kernel \(K(r) \sim r^{-1-\mu}\) with \(\mu < 2\) the diffusion becomes anomalous and the exponent generalises to \(z = \mu/(2\mu + 4)\), matching observation for oceanic communities where \(\mu \approx 1\).

title: 4  Multiple species and neutral theory
text:
4.9 Callouts






Neutral theory is a null model. When it fits, we cannot conclude that species are ecologically equivalent — only that whatever differences exist are not visible in the SAD.









When analysing a new biodiversity dataset, always fit the neutral model first. A model of niches, competition, or environmental filtering is only worth building if it out-performs the two-parameter neutral baseline.









Neutral theory correctly predicts SADs but not the correlations between species. When a study reports strong species-species correlations, non-neutral mechanisms are usually needed.









The scaling exponent \(z\) is robust — it takes similar values across datasets — but the fitted \(\theta\) and \(m\) are not: they depend on the sampling scheme. Report both when publishing.

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.1 The Lotka–Volterra equations
Neutral theory (Chapter 3) tells us how much of an ecological pattern can be explained by demographic noise alone. To move beyond it we now add the biological content that neutral theory deliberately ignores: species interact. This chapter builds up from the classical Lotka–Volterra system, generalises it to arbitrarily many species, and shows how the celebrated May stability paradox leads directly to random matrix theory.
For two species — predator \(y\) and prey \(x\) — the deterministic Lotka–Volterra system is \[\dot x = \alpha x - \beta x y, \qquad \dot y = \delta x y - \gamma y ,\] with all four rate constants positive. Trajectories are closed orbits around the neutral fixed point \((x^*, y^*) = (\gamma/\delta, \alpha/\beta)\).
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
For \(S\) species with abundances \(\mathbf x = (x_1, \ldots, x_S)\) the generalised Lotka–Volterra equations are \[\dot x_i = x_i\left(r_i + \sum_{j=1}^{S} \alpha_{ij}\,x_j\right), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, S,\] where \(r_i\) is the intrinsic growth rate of species \(i\) and \(\alpha_{ij}\) is the per-capita effect of species \(j\) on species \(i\). Diagonal entries \(\alpha_{ii} < 0\) encode intra-specific competition.


The interior fixed point \(\mathbf x^*\) of GLV satisfies \(\mathbf r + A\mathbf x^* = 0\), i.e. \(\mathbf x^* = -A^{-1}\mathbf r\). Linearising around \(\mathbf x^*\) gives the Jacobian \(J = \text{diag}(\mathbf x^*)\,A\), so stability of \(\mathbf x^*\) is governed by the eigenvalues of a weighted version of the interaction matrix.


Remark. GLV is the workhorse model of community ecology because it reproduces the three qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes (fixed point, limit cycle, chaos) with a single interaction matrix. It also emerges as the quasi-steady-state limit of many consumer–resource models.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.2 Stochastic Volterra model
Adding demographic noise to Lotka–Volterra gives the stochastic model \[dx_i = x_i\Bigl(r_i + \sum_j \alpha_{ij} x_j\Bigr) dt + \sqrt{2 D_i x_i}\,dW_i(t),\] whose power spectrum shows stochastic oscillations even in parameter regimes where the deterministic model has a stable fixed point.

Around a stable interior fixed point \(\mathbf x^*\), linearised fluctuations \(\delta \mathbf x(t) = \mathbf x(t) - \mathbf x^*\) satisfy \[d\delta\mathbf x = J\,\delta\mathbf x\,dt + \Sigma^{1/2}\,d\mathbf W(t) ,\] with \(J = \text{diag}(\mathbf x^*)A\). The Fourier power spectrum of \(\delta x_i\) is \[S_{ii}(\omega) = \sum_{jk}\bigl[(J - i\omega I)^{-1}\bigr]_{ij}\bigl[(J + i\omega I)^{-1}\bigr]_{ik} \Sigma_{jk} ,\] which typically has a peak at a non-zero \(\omega\) — the stochastic amplification of a mode that would decay deterministically.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
section: 5.3 Random interactions and the May paradox
text:
5.3 Random interactions and the May paradox
If \(S \gg 1\) the biologist is confronted with \(S^2\) interaction coefficients, which cannot possibly be estimated one by one. Robert May’s insight (1972) was to sidestep the details and ask: what does a “typical” interaction matrix imply for stability?

Consider a community of \(S\) species with random pairwise interactions: \[A_{ij} = -\delta_{ij} + \sigma\,c\,g_{ij}, \qquad g_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\text{ i.i.d.\ off-diagonal},\] where \(c \in [0, 1]\) is the connectance (fraction of non-zero entries) and \(\sigma\) the interaction strength. The diagonal encodes self-regulation.


The community defined above is stable with high probability in the limit \(S \to \infty\) if and only if \[\sigma\sqrt{cS} < 1 .\] Equivalently, if the “complexity” \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}\) exceeds one, the interior fixed point loses stability and the community can undergo cycles or extinctions.

The theorem is proved by observing that the eigenvalues of \(A\) concentrate on a disc in the complex plane of radius \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}\) centred at \(-1\) (the circular law), so the rightmost eigenvalue crosses zero exactly at the threshold above.

Among the three parameters \((S, c, \sigma)\), stability is preserved by decreasing interaction strength or connectance, but not by adding more species. Real ecosystems appear to escape this trade-off by having structured, non-random interaction networks.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.4 Proof idea: the circular law
The key tool behind May’s result is the circular law of random matrix theory:

Let \(M\) be an \(S \times S\) matrix with entries i.i.d. with zero mean and variance \(1/S\). In the limit \(S \to \infty\), the empirical spectral distribution of \(M\) converges (weakly, almost surely) to the uniform distribution on the unit disc in \(\mathbb C\).

Applied to the shifted matrix \(A + I\), the circular law gives eigenvalues uniformly on the disc of radius \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}\), whose real part is bounded above by that radius.

For a Gaussian \(M\) the spectral density can be derived explicitly using a Coulomb-gas / replica calculation. The joint density of eigenvalues in the complex plane is \[P(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_S) \propto \prod_{i<j} |\lambda_i - \lambda_j|^2\,\prod_k e^{-S|\lambda_k|^2} .\] Interpreted as a 2D Coulomb gas at temperature \(1/S\), the distribution flattens into the uniform disc as \(S \to \infty\).


The replica trick evaluates \(\langle \ln \det(zI - M)\rangle\) by writing \(\ln x = \lim_{n\to 0}(x^n - 1)/n\), promoting the average of the \(n\)-th power of the determinant to a Gaussian integral, and solving the saddle-point at large \(S\). The trick was invented for spin glasses (Sherrington–Kirkpatrick) but reappears everywhere random matrices show up — including in the neural chapters below.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.5 Structured interactions
Real ecosystems are neither i.i.d. nor mean-field. Two forms of structure matter most:

Let the off-diagonal entries of \(A\) be jointly Gaussian with variance \(\sigma^2\) and correlation \(\rho = \text{corr}(A_{ij}, A_{ji})\). Then the spectrum lies on an ellipse of semi-axes \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}(1 + \rho)\) and \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}(1 - \rho)\). Predator–prey communities (\(\rho < 0\)) tend to be more stable than mutualistic ones (\(\rho > 0\)) for the same complexity.

Empirical food webs show strongly negative \(\rho\): whenever species \(j\) affects \(i\), the reverse effect \(A_{ji}\) has the opposite sign. This is one of the main reasons real ecosystems can be much larger than May’s threshold suggests.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.6 Mutualism, competition, and food webs
Beyond pairwise correlations, network structure — who interacts with whom — is decisive.

Empirical plant–pollinator networks are highly nested: specialists interact with a subset of the partners of generalists. Nested networks concentrate spectral mass and give a lower principal eigenvalue than random networks of the same \(S\) and \(c\), so they can be more stable than uncorrelated matrices. Bastolla et al. (2009) argue this explains why mutualistic communities persist at complexities where May’s threshold would predict collapse.


Remark (Adaptive stability). Species evolve. If the interaction matrix \(A\) is itself a slow variable driven by selection for stability, the community can self-organise into a stable configuration even if a random \(A\) of the same statistics would not be. This is the adaptive or evolutionary form of the complexity–stability question.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.7 Competitive exclusion
Finally, the classic result of Gause: two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot coexist at equilibrium. In GLV form, if two species \(i, j\) have identical growth requirements (\(r_i / \alpha_{ii} = r_j/\alpha_{jj}\) and identical impact on the resource), the equilibrium is a one-parameter family, and any small perturbation drives one to extinction. The generalisation to \(S\) species and \(R\) resources gives:

In a purely resource-mediated community, the number of coexisting species at equilibrium cannot exceed the number of independent limiting resources: \(S_{coex} \le R\).

Nature routinely exceeds this bound (the plankton paradox); the tools of the previous section — noise, non-equilibrium dynamics, network structure — are how the paradox is resolved.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.8 Exercises

Show that the two-species Lotka–Volterra system is Hamiltonian: find conserved quantities \(H(x, y)\) such that \(\dot H = 0\). Sketch the phase portrait.


Solution. Multiply \(\dot x/x = \alpha - \beta y\) by \(\delta\) and \(\dot y/y = -\gamma + \delta x\) by \(\beta\) and add: \[\delta \dot x /x + \beta \dot y /y = \delta \alpha - \gamma \beta,\] so \(H(x, y) = \delta x - \gamma \ln x + \beta y - \alpha \ln y\) is conserved along trajectories. Level sets are closed curves around the fixed point \((x^*, y^*) = (\gamma/\delta, \alpha/\beta)\).


Verify May’s threshold numerically: for \(S = 100\), \(c = 0.5\), sweep \(\sigma\) from \(0.05\) to \(0.3\) and estimate the fraction of \(10^3\) random matrices whose principal eigenvalue crosses zero. Compare with the analytical threshold.


Solution. The theoretical threshold is \(\sigma^* = 1/\sqrt{cS} \approx 0.141\). A numerical experiment sampling \(\sigma\,g_{ij}\) with \(g_{ij}\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) shows a sharp transition of the “stable” fraction from \(\approx 1\) to \(\approx 0\) within a window \(\sigma^* \pm 0.02\), in agreement with the finite-\(S\) correction predicted by the Tracy–Widom distribution.
crumbs: 5  Species interactions and random matrices

title: 5  Species interactions and random matrices
text:
5.9 Callouts






May’s paradox is not a proof that ecosystems collapse; it is a proof that random ecosystems collapse. The next generation of ecological modelling is about which network structures escape it.









When simulating GLV, keep the diagonal of \(A\) strictly negative and of order \(-1\): this fixes the noise scale so that different \((S, c, \sigma)\) triples are directly comparable.









“Complexity” in ecology has three technical meanings that are often conflated: species richness \(S\), connectance \(c\), and interaction strength \(\sigma\). May’s result is about their product \(\sigma\sqrt{cS}\), not about any of them alone.









The circular law relies on i.i.d. entries. Any structured pattern (block-diagonal, nested, phylogenetically constrained) breaks the assumption and changes the effective threshold. Don’t apply May’s formula to real food-web data without accounting for structure.

title: 6  Introduction to neural systems
text:
6.1 5.1 The brain as a complex system
Part I of the course used ecology as the arena for statistical-physics modelling of complex systems. Part II changes scale: from populations of organisms to populations of neurons. This chapter mirrors Prof. Suweis’s Chapter 5 and sets the stage.
The brain contains roughly \(10^{11}\) neurons, each with roughly \(10^3\) synaptic connections — about \(10^{14}\) links in total. No description at the level of an isolated neuron can explain what the brain does. Function is emergent: it arises from the interactions.
Two paradigmatic emergent phenomena will occupy the second half of the course.

title: 6  Introduction to neural systems
text:
The brain is a complex system in the technical sense of Chapter 1: many simple units, sparse but strong local interactions, ubiquitous noise, and observables (perception, memory, decision) that only exist at the ensemble level.



Data can be subdivided into time windows \([t_i, t_i + \Delta t]\). An avalanche is a burst of activity spanning consecutive windows each with at least one spike. Its size \(s\) is the number of active neurons summed over the burst. The distribution of \(s\) measured in cortical cultures follows a power law \[p(s) \propto s^{-3/2}\] over several decades, with a finite-size cutoff at \(s \sim N\) (the total number of neurons). We will see in Chapter 10 that this exponent is the mean-field directed-percolation value — evidence for brain criticality.


Sustained oscillations at specific frequencies — delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (12–30 Hz), gamma (30–100 Hz) — correlate with distinct cognitive states (sleep, learning, alertness). Sustained oscillations require synchronisation of large populations of neurons and are a paradigmatic example of self-organising collective behaviour.

title: 6  Introduction to neural systems
text:
6.2 5.2 Measurements
Measurements of neural activity span an enormous range of spatial and temporal resolution. It is useful to categorise the tools by their scale.

6.2.1 Non-invasive techniques (whole-brain, coarse)

Electroencephalography (EEG). Electrodes on the scalp measure the local electrical fields produced by large populations of synchronously-firing neurons. Millisecond time resolution but only centimetre spatial resolution; source localisation (the inverse problem) is intrinsically ill-posed.
Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI). MRI-based technique that tracks the anisotropic diffusion of water along white-matter axon bundles, yielding a mesoscopic map of the anatomical (structural) brain connectivity.
Functional MRI (fMRI). Measures the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal — a proxy for local metabolic demand — with \(\sim\) mm spatial resolution but only \(\sim\) s temporal resolution. Used to construct functional connectivity matrices.



6.2.2 Invasive techniques (few-neuron, fine)

Neuro-probes. Micro-electrodes are inserted into brain tissue and record intracellular or extracellular voltage. Single-cell precision but limited to a few units at a time.
In-vitro cultures. Dissociated neurons are plated on a multi-electrode array; the microscopic dynamics of a small network is observed under controlled conditions.
Fluorescence calcium imaging. Genetically encoded calcium indicators (e.g. GCaMP) fluoresce when a neuron spikes. Modern implementations image thousands of neurons simultaneously at cellular resolution, driving the current revolution in systems neuroscience.


Remark (Multi-scale modelling). The multi-scale measurements motivate multi-scale modelling: Chapter 6 treats a single neuron as an electrical circuit; Chapter 7 treats a population of neurons as a rate variable; Chapter 8 introduces plasticity that lets networks learn; Chapter 9 introduces stochastic recurrent networks (Boltzmann machines); Chapter 10 puts everything together and asks whether the healthy brain sits at a critical point.

title: 6  Introduction to neural systems
text:
6.3 Road map for Part II
The rest of the course threads the following logic:

Chapter 6 — dynamics of a single neuron. Structure (soma, dendrites, axon, synapses), membrane potential, ionic pumps, the action potential, spike-count/firing rate, response functions, tuning curves; then bio-electrophysiological models (Hodgkin–Huxley, integrate-and-fire) and the McCulloch–Pitts abstraction.
Chapter 7 — firing-rate networks. Wilson–Cowan and its bifurcations; recurrent networks; linear rate networks and their spectrum; stochastic rate models and avalanche statistics.
Chapter 8 — plasticity and Hopfield. Hebbian rule, subtractive normalisation, associative memory, the Hopfield energy landscape, capacity, and reservoir computing.
Chapter 9 — Boltzmann machines. Stochastic Hopfield dynamics, contrastive divergence, restricted Boltzmann machines.
Chapter 10 — brain criticality. Neural avalanches revisited, the Haldeman–Beggs (HTC) model on structural connectomes, continuous-time approximation, thermodynamic limit.







The chapter is phenomenological — it introduces vocabulary rather than mathematical machinery. All formal statements are proved in the following chapters.









When reading the neural literature, always check which signal is being measured (spikes vs LFP vs BOLD) and which scale is being modelled (single neuron vs population vs whole brain). Cross-scale claims are the source of most controversies.









The observation of power-law avalanches, \(p(s) \sim s^{-3/2}\), is necessary but not sufficient evidence of criticality. Chapter 10 discusses statistical tests (Clauset–Shalizi–Newman) that distinguish true criticality from apparent power laws.

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
7.1 6.1 The neuron
Before we build networks we need to understand what one node does. This chapter mirrors Prof. Suweis’s Chapter 6: cellular structure and membrane potential; firing rate as a response to a stimulus; the bio-electrophysiological (Hodgkin–Huxley) description; and the McCulloch–Pitts abstraction that will underlie all networks in Chapters 7–9.
Neurons are cells specialised for propagating signals over long distances. Their morphology has three functional parts:
The resting potential is maintained by ion pumps and channels in the cell membrane that create concentration gradients of Na\(^+\), K\(^+\), Ca\(^{2+}\) and Cl\(^-\). In particular, K\(^+\) is more concentrated inside the neuron and Na\(^+\) more concentrated outside.
When depolarisation pushes \(V\) above a threshold \(V_{th} \approx -55\) mV, the neuron fires an action potential — a stereotyped \(\sim 100\) mV pulse of \(\sim 1\) ms duration that propagates along the axon.
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
Dendrites — highly branched extensions that receive input signals from \(\sim 10^4\) other neurons through synapses.
Soma (cell body) — houses the nucleus; integrates the incoming currents.
Axon — a single, often very long (\(\gtrsim\) 1 m in some sensory neurons), extension that carries the output signal to downstream neurons.


The membrane potential \(V\) is the electrical potential inside the cell relative to the extracellular medium. Under resting conditions \(V_{\text{rest}} \approx -70\) mV. The cell is then said to be polarised.




Current in the form of positive ions flowing out of the cell (or negative ions flowing in) drives \(V\) more negative: hyperpolarisation.
Current into the cell drives \(V\) less negative or positive: depolarisation.




Remark. The action potential’s shape is very nearly the same every time; the information the neuron transmits is coded in the timing of spikes (rate code, temporal code), not in their amplitude. This is the “all-or-none” principle established by Adrian in the 1920s and mathematised by Hodgkin & Huxley in the 1950s.
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
section: 7.2 6.2 Neuron firing as response to a stimulus
text:
7.2 6.2 Neuron firing as response to a stimulus
Given an input stimulus \(s(t)\) we ask: what is the spike output? Model the spike train as a sum of Dirac deltas:

Given spike times \(\{t_i\}_{i=1}^n\) in an interval \([0, T]\), the neural response function is \[\rho(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \delta(t - t_i) .\] For any test function \(h(\tau)\) the convolution \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} h(t - t_i) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} h(\tau)\,\rho(t - \tau)\,d\tau\] converts the spike train into a smooth signal.


The spike-count rate on a window \([0, T]\) is \[r = \frac{n}{T} = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \rho(\tau)\,d\tau .\] The time-dependent firing rate \(\phi(t)\) is the running average of \(\rho\) over a moving window; formally \[\phi(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{1}{\Delta t}\,\mathbb E\!\left[\int_{t - \Delta t /2}^{t + \Delta t/2}\rho(\tau)\,d\tau\right] .\]

For a stationary point process \(\phi(t) = \lambda\) is the intensity.

For a sensory neuron responding to an oriented visual stimulus, the firing rate as a function of orientation \(\theta\) is a bell-shaped tuning curve: \[\phi(\theta) = \phi_{\max}\exp\!\bigl(-(\theta - \theta^*)^2/(2\sigma^2)\bigr),\] where \(\theta^*\) is the preferred orientation. Cataloguing tuning curves is a workhorse method of systems neuroscience.
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
7.3 6.3 Bio-electrophysiological modelling of the neuron
To go beyond phenomenology we need a physical model of the membrane. The membrane behaves as a capacitor with parallel-conductance ion channels:

For a passive patch of membrane, \[C_m\,\frac{dV}{dt} = -g_L(V - V_L) + I(t) ,\] where \(C_m\) is the membrane capacitance, \(g_L\) the leak conductance, \(V_L\) the leak reversal potential, and \(I(t)\) the input current. In the absence of active channels, the membrane behaves as a low-pass filter with time constant \(\tau_m = C_m/g_L \approx 10{-}30\) ms.


Adding voltage-gated Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\) conductances, whose gating variables \(m, h, n\) obey first-order kinetics, gives \[C_m\,\frac{dV}{dt} = -g_{Na}\,m^3 h\,(V - V_{Na}) - g_K\,n^4\,(V - V_K) - g_L(V - V_L) + I(t),\] with \(\dot m = \alpha_m(V)(1 - m) - \beta_m(V)m\), and analogous for \(h, n\). The four-dimensional system exhibits an excitable regime with an action potential and a stable refractory period.

The Hodgkin–Huxley model won its authors the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology and remains the biophysical gold standard.

For network-scale modelling the Hodgkin–Huxley description is impractical. The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron replaces the spike-generating dynamics by a threshold: integrate the passive RC equation until \(V\) crosses \(V_{th}\), emit a spike, reset \(V \to V_{reset}\), and impose a refractory period \(\tau_{ref}\). LIF captures the essential firing behaviour with a single ODE and one non-linearity.


For a LIF neuron driven by a constant current \(I_0 > (V_{th} - V_L)g_L\), the interspike interval is \[\Delta t = \tau_m\,\ln\!\left(\frac{I_0/g_L - (V_{reset} - V_L)}{I_0/g_L - (V_{th} - V_L)}\right),\] so the firing rate is \(\phi(I_0) = 1/\Delta t\). This is the rate transfer function used in Wilson–Cowan (Chapter 7).
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
7.4 6.4 McCulloch–Pitts artificial neuron
For network-scale mathematical modelling we abstract even further. McCulloch & Pitts (1943) proposed the following:

A McCulloch–Pitts neuron with \(N\) inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_N\) (each 0 or 1), synaptic weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_N\), and threshold \(\theta\) produces output \[y = \Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,x_i - \theta\right) \in \{0, 1\},\] where \(\Theta\) is the Heaviside step function.

The McCulloch–Pitts unit is the fundamental building block of every neural network in this course.

With appropriate weights and threshold, a single McCulloch–Pitts unit computes any two-input Boolean function except XOR. A two-layer network of such units can compute XOR — the classic Minsky–Papert observation that motivated multi-layer networks.


Remark. The step-function activation of the McCulloch–Pitts unit was replaced in modern practice by the sigmoid \(\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})\) (allowing gradient-based learning) and later by ReLU \(\max(0, x)\) (avoiding vanishing gradients in deep networks). Both are approximations of the biological non-linearity.
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
7.5 Exercises

Derive the LIF firing rate under constant current given above. State the parameter regime where the neuron fires periodically.


Solution. Solve \(C_m \dot V = -g_L(V - V_L) + I_0\) with initial condition \(V(0) = V_{reset}\) and first-passage condition \(V(\Delta t) = V_{th}\). The solution is \(V(t) = V_\infty + (V_{reset} - V_\infty)e^{-t/\tau_m}\) with \(V_\infty = V_L + I_0/g_L\). Setting \(V(\Delta t) = V_{th}\) and solving for \(\Delta t\) gives the formula. The neuron fires periodically iff \(V_\infty > V_{th}\), i.e. \(I_0 > (V_{th} - V_L)g_L\).


Show that no single McCulloch–Pitts unit implements the XOR function on two inputs.


Solution. Suppose weights \(w_1, w_2\) and threshold \(\theta\) give XOR. Then \(w_1 + w_2 \le \theta - 1\) (input \((1,1)\) outputs 0), but each of \(w_1, w_2 > \theta - 1\) (inputs \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) output 1). Summing: \(w_1 + w_2 > 2\theta - 2\). Combining with \(w_1 + w_2 \le \theta - 1\): \(\theta - 1 > 2\theta - 2\), i.e. \(\theta < 1\). But also \((0,0)\) must output 0, so \(\theta > 0\). Both bounds together give \(0 < \theta < 1\). Now check \((0, 1)\): need \(w_2 > \theta > 0\), and \((1, 1)\): \(w_1 + w_2 \le \theta - 1 < 0\). So \(w_1 < -w_2 < -\theta < 0\). Then \((1, 0)\): \(w_1 < 0 < \theta\), so output is 0, not 1. Contradiction.


Verify that the leak time constant \(\tau_m = C_m / g_L\) has units of time given typical values \(C_m \sim 10^{-6}\,\text{F/cm}^2\) and \(g_L \sim 10^{-4}\,\text{S/cm}^2\).


Solution. \(C/g = \text{F/S} = (\text{C/V})/(1/\text{Ω}) = \text{C}\cdot\text{Ω/V} = \text{s}\) (since \(\text{V} = \text{Ω A} = \text{Ω C/s}\)). Numerically \(\tau_m = 10^{-2}\) s = 10 ms, matching biology.
crumbs: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron

title: 7  Dynamics of a single neuron
text:
7.6 Callouts






The three levels of description — Hodgkin–Huxley, integrate-and-fire, McCulloch–Pitts — represent decreasing biological fidelity but increasing analytical tractability. Which one to use depends on the question you are asking.









For any rate model of a network, first sketch the transfer function \(\phi(I)\) of a single neuron. Its shape (linear-rectifier, sigmoidal, threshold-linear) will determine the qualitative regimes of the network.









The action potential is stereotyped: its amplitude carries no information. This is the reason firing-rate models exist — throwing away the details of each spike loses little.









The LIF neuron has a hard reset that removes any memory of the spike time; a soft-reset LIF (subtract \(V_{th} - V_{reset}\)) can produce very different collective dynamics near the firing threshold.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.1 Rate versus spike models
We now switch scale: from populations of species to populations of neurons. The ecological toolkit — mean-field ODEs, master equations, mean-field random matrices — carries over almost unchanged, and the first stop is the firing-rate model, the simplest description of neural population activity.
Individual neurons emit action potentials — stereotyped voltage pulses of \(\sim 1\) ms duration. When many neurons fire the informative signal is not the timing of each spike but the rate \(\phi(t)\) at which spikes are emitted in a short window. Firing-rate models replace the discrete spike train by this continuous rate.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
The firing rate of a neuron is \[\phi(t) = \frac{\text{number of spikes in a window } [t - \Delta/2,\, t + \Delta/2]}{\Delta},\] in the limit \(\Delta \to 0\) after ensemble-averaging over trials. For a stationary point process \(\phi(t) = \lambda\) is the intensity of the spike train.


Remark. For most biophysical purposes the rate description is valid whenever the network activity varies on timescales \(\gg 1/\lambda\). Below that scale (single-spike coincidence coding) rate models fail and one must go back to spike-timing models such as leaky integrate-and-fire.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.2 Excitatory–inhibitory populations
Even before we introduce networks, the effective single-population equation is instructive. Let \(\phi(t)\) be the mean rate of a homogeneous population; the deterministic rate equation is \[\tau\,\dot \phi = -\phi + F(I),\] where \(I\) is the input current and \(F\) is a monotone gain function (the transfer function), typically sigmoidal.
The next level of realism separates the population into excitatory (\(E\)) and inhibitory (\(I\)) sub-populations that interact via signed synapses:

The Wilson–Cowan equations for the mean firing rates of coupled excitatory and inhibitory populations are \[\begin{aligned}
\tau_E\,\dot\phi_E &= -\phi_E + F_E\bigl(W_{EE}\phi_E - W_{EI}\phi_I + I_E^{ext}\bigr),\\
\tau_I\,\dot\phi_I &= -\phi_I + F_I\bigl(W_{IE}\phi_E - W_{II}\phi_I + I_I^{ext}\bigr).
\end{aligned}\] The four constants \(W_{XY} > 0\) encode the average synaptic weights between populations; \(F_{E,I}\) are sigmoid transfer functions saturating at some maximum rate.


The Wilson–Cowan system exhibits three qualitatively different regimes: (i) a single stable low-activity fixed point (rest state); (ii) two stable fixed points separated by a saddle (bistability, working memory); (iii) a Hopf-bifurcated limit cycle (oscillation). The transitions occur along a cusp in the \((I_E, I_I)\) external-input plane.


Wilson–Cowan networks with excitatory time constant \(\tau_E \sim 5\) ms and inhibitory \(\tau_I \sim 10\) ms show a Hopf bifurcation to oscillations at \(\sim 40\) Hz — the gamma rhythm implicated in perceptual binding and attention. The oscillation frequency depends on the lag between E and I responses, not on any individual neuron’s intrinsic frequency.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.3 Recurrent networks
A more microscopic description replaces the two lumped populations by \(N\) individual rate units: \[\tau\,\dot\phi_i = -\phi_i + F\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{N} W_{ij}\phi_j + I_i^{ext}\Bigr), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, N.\] When \(W\) is a full matrix this is a recurrent rate network — the object of the rest of the chapter.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.4 Linear recurrent networks
Suppose \(F\) is linear, \(F(x) = x\). Then the dynamics is \[\tau\,\dot{\boldsymbol\phi} = (W - I)\boldsymbol\phi + \mathbf I^{ext} .\] The behaviour is governed by the spectrum of \(W\):

The linear rate network is stable if and only if the leading eigenvalue of \(W\) has real part less than \(1\). If \(W\) is drawn from the May ensemble of Chapter 4 with parameters \((N, c, \sigma)\), the leading eigenvalue is \(\sigma\sqrt{cN}\); the network is stable iff \(\sigma\sqrt{cN} < 1\), exactly the ecological threshold.

The equivalence between May’s stability criterion and the transition to chaos in random recurrent networks is one of the most striking cross-domain results in the notes: Sompolinsky, Crisanti and Sommers (1988) proved that a nonlinear random rate network transitions from a fixed point to deterministic chaos exactly at \(\sigma\sqrt{N} = 1\).

For a nonlinear rate network with \(W_{ij}\) i.i.d. Gaussian of variance \(\sigma^2/N\) and gain function \(\phi = \tanh(x)\), the fixed point at zero loses stability at \(\sigma = 1\). For \(\sigma > 1\) the dynamics is deterministically chaotic, with a positive Lyapunov exponent that grows continuously from zero.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.5 Stochastic rate networks
Adding noise to the rate equation gives a Langevin picture: \[d\phi_i = \tau^{-1}\bigl(-\phi_i + F(\sum_j W_{ij}\phi_j)\bigr)\,dt + \sigma_\eta\,dW_i(t).\] For a linear \(F\) the process is Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, and its power spectrum is \[S(\omega) = \frac{2\sigma_\eta^2\,\tau^2}{|(W - I)\tau + i\omega\tau I|^2 + \omega^2\tau^2},\] generalising the stochastic-Volterra result of Chapter 4.

Near the stability boundary \(\sigma\sqrt{cN} = 1\), the linear stochastic rate network shows avalanches of bursty activity whose size distribution follows a power law \(P(s) \sim s^{-3/2}\), characteristic of a critical branching process. This has been proposed as a mechanism for the empirically observed avalanche statistics in cortical recordings.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.6 Exercises

Derive the mean-field fixed point of a Wilson–Cowan network with symmetric parameters \(\tau_E = \tau_I\), \(W_{EE} = W_{II} = 0\), \(W_{EI} = W_{IE} = w > 0\), and no external input. When does a Hopf bifurcation occur as \(w\) is increased?


Solution. The fixed points satisfy \(\phi_E = F(-w\phi_I)\) and \(\phi_I = F(w\phi_E)\). If \(F\) is odd, \(\phi_E = -\phi_I\) is a solution which, for \(F(x) = \tanh(x)\), gives \(\phi_E = \tanh(w\phi_E)\): only \(\phi_E = 0\) if \(w < 1\); two symmetric nontrivial roots for \(w > 1\). Linearising around \((0,0)\): eigenvalues of the Jacobian are \(\pm i w F'(0)\), so at \(w F'(0) = 1\) we have a pure imaginary pair — the Hopf point. For \(w > w_c\) a limit cycle grows out of it.


Show that the transition to chaos in the Sompolinsky–Crisanti–Sommers network can be understood as a growth of the largest Lyapunov exponent from zero. Use the dynamic mean-field theory to write a self-consistent equation for the autocorrelation \(C(t) = \langle \phi_i(t')\phi_i(t' + t)\rangle\).


Solution. The dynamic mean-field ansatz replaces the recurrent input to any neuron by a Gaussian field with the same auto-covariance. Writing \(\phi_i(t) = F(x_i(t))\) with \(\langle x_i(t) x_i(t')\rangle = \sigma^2 C_\phi(t - t')\), self-consistency gives \[C_\phi(\tau) = \int \tanh(\sqrt{\sigma^2 C_\phi(0)}\,z_1)\tanh(\sqrt{\sigma^2 C_\phi(0)}\,z_2)\,d\mathcal N,\] which is a fixed-point equation for the correlation function. Its trivial solution \(C_\phi \equiv 0\) becomes unstable at \(\sigma = 1\); a nontrivial oscillating solution grows continuously above threshold, matching the Lyapunov diagnosis.

title: 8  Firing-rate networks
text:
8.7 Callouts






Firing-rate models describe populations, not single neurons. Predictions such as gamma oscillations or avalanches are about ensembles; single-neuron voltage traces look nothing like their solutions.









The single most useful check on any recurrent-network simulation is the eigenvalue spectrum of \(W\): if the leading eigenvalue’s real part exceeds one, the linear part is already unstable and the dynamics you are seeing is dominated by the nonlinearity, not by the network you intended to model.









The result “power-law avalanches with exponent \(-3/2\)” appears in many neuroscience datasets. It is not by itself evidence of criticality: a wide variety of non-critical processes produce the same exponent.

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.1 Hebbian plasticity
The synapses \(W_{ij}\) of Chapter 7 were fixed. In real brains they change — that is plasticity — and the pattern of changes lets the network store and retrieve information. This chapter mirrors Prof. Suweis’s Chapter 8: Hebbian plasticity and its subtractively-normalised variant, associative-memory networks, and the Hopfield model with its statistical-mechanical analysis. The extension to stochastic recurrent networks (Boltzmann machines) is treated separately in Chapter 9.
The essence of Hebb’s rule is captured in the slogan “neurons that fire together, wire together”. Formally:
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
Let \(\phi_i, \phi_j\) be the firing rates of two neurons and \(W_{ij}\) the weight of the synapse from \(j\) to \(i\). The Hebbian rule is \[\tau_W\,\dot W_{ij} = \eta\,\phi_i\,\phi_j ,\] with learning rate \(\eta > 0\). Under repeated correlated activity of pre- and post-synaptic neurons, \(W_{ij}\) grows without bound.


Remark. The unbounded growth is unphysical: real synaptic weights are bounded. Two standard fixes are (i) subtractive normalisation — subtract the mean activity from each factor; (ii) multiplicative normalisation (Oja’s rule) — subtract a term proportional to \(\phi_i^2 W_{ij}\) that stabilises the norm.


Under the subtractively normalised Hebbian rule with a linear rate unit driven by inputs \(\mathbf x(t)\), the synaptic weight vector converges to the leading eigenvector of the input covariance \(\Sigma = \langle \mathbf x \mathbf x^\top\rangle\). Hebbian plasticity therefore performs principal component analysis.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.2 Associative memory networks
Suppose we want the network to remember a set of patterns \(\{\boldsymbol\xi^\mu\}_{\mu=1}^{P}\), each a vector of \(N\) binary units \(\xi_i^\mu \in \{-1, +1\}\). The Hebbian prescription is:

Given patterns \(\boldsymbol\xi^\mu\), the Hebbian synaptic matrix is \[W_{ij} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mu=1}^{P}\xi_i^\mu\,\xi_j^\mu, \qquad W_{ii} = 0 .\] The network dynamics is \(s_i(t+1) = \text{sgn}\bigl(\sum_j W_{ij}\,s_j(t)\bigr)\). A pattern \(\boldsymbol\xi^\mu\) is stored if it is a fixed point of these dynamics.

This construction is the Hopfield network. Its analysis, unlike the recurrent nets of Chapter 5, is statistical-mechanical: the dynamics has a Lyapunov function, so a temperature can be introduced by hand and the equilibrium ensemble studied.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.3 Hopfield energy landscape

For the Hopfield model with symmetric weights \(W_{ij} = W_{ji}\) and zero diagonal, the quantity \[H[\mathbf s] = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij} W_{ij}\,s_i\,s_j\] is monotonically non-increasing under synchronous or asynchronous sign updates. Fixed points are local minima of \(H\).

The stored patterns \(\boldsymbol\xi^\mu\) are, by construction, minima of \(H\). But the Hebbian rule also creates spurious minima — combinations like \(\text{sgn}(\xi^{\mu_1} + \xi^{\mu_2} + \xi^{\mu_3})\) that are also local minima of \(H\), but do not correspond to any single stored pattern.

The maximum number of patterns that can be stored and retrieved reliably in a Hopfield network of \(N\) binary units is \[P_{\max} \approx 0.138\,N .\] Beyond this critical loading \(\alpha_c = P/N \approx 0.138\), retrieval fails: a spin-glass phase takes over in which memory patterns cease to be attractors.

The threshold \(\alpha_c\) is not a hand-wavy back-of-the-envelope result; it comes from the replica-symmetric solution of the Hopfield model treated as a spin glass.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
section: 9.4 Statistical mechanics of the Hopfield model
text:
9.4 Statistical mechanics of the Hopfield model
At temperature \(T = 1/\beta\) the Hopfield model is a disordered Ising system with couplings \(W_{ij}\) built from random patterns. The partition function is \[Z(\beta, \{\boldsymbol\xi\}) = \sum_{\mathbf s}e^{-\beta H[\mathbf s]}.\] Averaging \(\ln Z\) over the quenched randomness of the patterns (as in Chapter 4’s replica trick) gives the free energy in terms of two order parameters: the overlaps \(m^\mu = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \xi_i^\mu s_i\) with each stored pattern, and the Edwards–Anderson order parameter \(q = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \langle s_i\rangle^2\) measuring frozen local magnetisation.

The \((T, \alpha)\) phase diagram of the Hopfield model has three phases:

Retrieval phase at low \(T\) and \(\alpha < \alpha_c(T)\): one \(m^\mu\) is \(O(1)\), memories are attractors.
Spin-glass phase at low \(T\) and \(\alpha > \alpha_c(T)\): all \(m^\mu = 0\) but \(q > 0\); memories are lost.
Paramagnetic phase at high \(T\): \(q = 0\); no correlations survive.

At \(T = 0\) the critical loading is \(\alpha_c = 0.138\).


Fixing \(\alpha < 0.138\) and cooling from high \(T\), the Hopfield network undergoes a second-order transition from paramagnet to retrieval phase at \(T_c(\alpha)\). Below \(T_c\) the network settles to a state with macroscopic overlap with a randomly chosen stored pattern. This is the physical mechanism of associative memory.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
section: 9.5 Supervised learning with recurrent networks (reservoir computing)
text:
9.5 Supervised learning with recurrent networks (reservoir computing)
An alternative to storing static patterns is to use the transient dynamics of a randomly connected recurrent network to represent inputs. This is the idea of reservoir computing (also known as an echo-state network or liquid-state machine):

Fix a large, random, sub-critical recurrent network with weights \(W\) (with \(\sigma\sqrt{N} < 1\) so activity decays). Drive it with a time-varying input \(\mathbf u(t)\). Train only a linear readout \(\mathbf y = C\,\boldsymbol\phi(t)\) to match a target signal \(\mathbf y^*(t)\).

Because only the readout is trained, the optimisation is convex (least squares) and does not suffer from vanishing gradients. Reservoirs poised near the edge of chaos (\(\sigma\sqrt N \approx 1\)) have the highest computational capacity — an application of the criticality theme from Chapter 4.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.6 Toward stochastic recurrent networks
The Hopfield model is deterministic: given the initial state, the trajectory is uniquely determined by the sign updates. Making it stochastic — the update is drawn from a Boltzmann distribution over the two options — gives the Boltzmann machine and connects the associative-memory picture to modern energy-based generative models. This extension is the subject of Chapter 9.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.7 Exercises

Verify that Oja’s rule \(\dot W = \eta(\phi \mathbf x - \phi^2 W)\) (with \(\phi = W^\top \mathbf x\)) drives \(W\) to unit norm and to the principal eigenvector of the input covariance.


Solution. Compute \(\dot{|W|^2} = 2 W^\top \dot W = 2\eta(\phi W^\top \mathbf x - \phi^2 |W|^2) = 2\eta\phi^2(1 - |W|^2)\): the norm relaxes to one. On the sphere, the fixed points satisfy \(\Sigma W = \lambda W\) with \(\lambda = W^\top \Sigma W\). Stability analysis shows that only the top eigenvector is stable.


Show that the Hopfield capacity \(\alpha_c \approx 0.138\) can be derived heuristically by demanding that the noise contribution to the local field on a pattern be smaller than the signal. Give the order-of-magnitude argument.


Solution. The local field on pattern \(\mu\) at site \(i\) is \(h_i^\mu = \xi_i^\mu + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\nu\neq\mu}\sum_j \xi_i^\nu \xi_j^\nu \xi_j^\mu\). The signal is \(\xi_i^\mu = \pm 1\) (variance 1); the noise is a sum of \(P - 1\) terms each of variance \(1/N\), so its variance is \((P-1)/N \sim \alpha\). Retrieval requires signal-to-noise \(> 1\), giving \(\alpha \lesssim 1\). The precise number \(0.138\) comes from a more careful replica calculation that accounts for correlations among the noise terms.
crumbs: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks

title: 9  Plasticity, associative memory and Hopfield networks
text:
9.8 Callouts






Hebbian plasticity is one of very few learning rules that is both biologically plausible and mathematically well-behaved. Most modern deep-learning algorithms (backprop) are neither.









When implementing a Hopfield network from scratch, always plot the energy \(H[\mathbf s(t)]\) during dynamics: monotone decrease is a necessary correctness check.









The Hopfield capacity \(\alpha_c \approx 0.138\) is the number of uncorrelated patterns that can be stored. Correlated patterns (e.g. real images) have a much lower effective capacity.









Real synapses are sign-constrained (Dale’s law) and typically bounded above by a saturation weight. The mathematical Hopfield model ignores both. Introducing these constraints reduces capacity and can change the phase diagram — see Brunel & Nadal (1998).
